> **[case-study]**
> **Paper Lane (PL)**
> 
> Paper Lane (PL) owns 48 shops in country D selling greetings cards, gift wrap, notebooks and pens. It employs 520 people.
> 
> Sales of greetings cards across country D have fallen for six years as more people send messages online. PL's notebook and pen sales have held steady.
> 
> PL's board has discussed four possible ways of growing, but has never used a formal framework to compare them:
> 
> - opening shops in a neighbouring country
> - selling personalised cards printed in store
> - persuading existing customers to visit more often
> - buying a chain of craft supply shops
> 
> **Table 1.1: PL selected data**
> 
> | Shops | 48 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 27 |
> | Share of revenue from greetings cards (%) | 58 |
> | Change in national greetings card sales over six years (%) | -31 |

Analyse **two** benefits to PL of using the Ansoff matrix to compare its growth options.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that the Ansoff matrix would let PL compare its four options on the same basis **[K]**. At present the board is weighing opening shops abroad against buying a craft chain and two other ideas, with no framework for judging them alongside one another **[Ap]**. Placing each option in the matrix shows at once that persuading existing customers to visit more often is market penetration, the lowest-risk route, while buying a craft chain is diversification, the highest **[An]**. Knowing which options carry the most risk lets PL rank them deliberately rather than adopting whichever idea is argued most persuasively at the meeting **[An]** A second benefit is that the matrix ties each option to PL's actual position **[K]**. Greetings cards provide 58% of PL's revenue in a national market that has shrunk by 31% over six years **[Ap]**. The matrix makes clear that market penetration means selling more of the same product in the same market, which only works where that market can support it, and PL's own figures show this one cannot **[An]**. That pushes the board towards options which change either the product or the market, so the framework rules out a route that looks safe but would leave PL tied ever more tightly to a declining product **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

> **[case-study]**
> **Iron Oak (IO)**
> 
> Iron Oak (IO) manufactures gym equipment for commercial fitness centres in country P. It makes treadmills, rowing machines and weight racks, and employs 310 people.
> 
> IO supplies around 700 fitness centres, many of which have bought from it for over a decade and trust its equipment to withstand heavy daily use.
> 
> Several of these customers have asked IO whether it plans to produce equipment that records each user's performance and sends it to a phone app. Two overseas manufacturers already sell such machines in country P.
> 
> IO employs no software engineers.
> 
> **Table 1.1: IO selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 310 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 44 |
> | Fitness centres supplied | 700 |
> | Estimated development cost (\$m) | 6.5 |
> | Estimated development time (years) | 2 |

Analyse **two** risks to IO of a product development strategy.
parts.solution_md:
One risk is that IO has no experience of the technology the new product would require **[K]**. IO employs 310 people making mechanical equipment and has no software engineers, yet connected machines depend on software that records performance and sends it to an app **[Ap]**. IO would have to recruit and manage skills it has never managed before, and a manufacturer unfamiliar with software is likely to underestimate how long development takes and how much testing it needs **[An]**. Delay matters particularly here, because two overseas manufacturers already sell connected machines in country P, so every extra month IO spends developing is a month those rivals spend winning over IO's own customers **[An]** A second risk is that IO must commit money long before it earns anything back **[K]**. Development is estimated at \$6.5m spread over about two years, a substantial commitment against annual revenue of \$44m **[Ap]**. Throughout those two years the money is going out while no connected machines are being sold, so IO's cash position weakens and its existing mechanical products must carry the whole business **[An]**. If the finished machines then fail to match what fitness centres expected, IO has no way of recovering the \$6.5m, having taken that risk on a product its customers merely asked about rather than committed to buying **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Open Road (OR)**
> 
> Open Road (OR) hires cars to leisure and business customers in country T. It operates 22 branches, mostly at airports and railway stations, and owns a fleet of 1,900 vehicles.
> 
> The car hire market in country T is not growing. OR competes with four other national firms offering similar cars at similar prices.
> 
> **Table 1.1: OR selected data**
> 
> | Branches | 22 |
> |---|---|
> | Vehicles owned | 1,900 |
> | Average vehicle utilisation (%) | 64 |
> | Share of the car hire market in country T (%) | 15 |
> | Customers who hired from OR more than once in 2025 (%) | 21 |
> 
> OR's marketing director has proposed a membership scheme giving repeat customers faster collection and a discount on their fourth hire of the year. She has also proposed advertising aimed at customers of rival firms.

Analyse **two** benefits to OR of a market penetration strategy.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that market penetration would raise the use OR gets from vehicles it already owns **[K]**. OR's fleet of 1,900 cars is hired out only 64% of the time, so around a third of it sits idle while still costing money in depreciation, insurance and storage **[Ap]**. Persuading existing customers to hire more often would fill some of that idle time without OR buying a single extra car, so nearly all of the additional revenue would go towards covering costs the business already carries **[An]**. Raising utilisation therefore improves OR's profit far faster than expanding the fleet would **[An]** A second benefit is that OR would be selling a service it already knows how to deliver **[K]**. The car hire market in country T is not growing, and OR competes with four national firms offering similar cars at similar prices **[Ap]**. A membership scheme rewarding a fourth hire gives customers a reason to come back to OR rather than compare prices afresh each time, which is one of the few ways to win share when the product itself is hard to make distinctive **[An]**. With only 21% of customers hiring more than once, even a modest rise in repeat business would lift revenue without the cost and uncertainty of entering a new market **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Silver Birch (SB)**
> 
> Silver Birch (SB) manufactures wooden children's toys in country E. It employs 130 people and sells through toy shops and department stores across country E only.
> 
> SB's toys are made from sustainably sourced timber and are known for lasting well enough to be passed from one child to the next.
> 
> The toy market in country E is mature, and SB's factory has spare room to produce more.
> 
> **Table 1.1: SB selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 12.4 |
> |---|---|
> | Annual sales growth in country E (%) | 2 |
> | Capacity utilisation (%) | 68 |
> | Number of countries SB currently sells in | 1 |
> | Enquiries from overseas retailers last year | 34 |
> 
> Two neighbouring countries have growing populations of young children and rising household incomes. Retailers in both contacted SB after seeing its products at a trade fair.
> 
> SB's directors are considering selling to these two countries using its existing range of toys.

Analyse **two** benefits to SB of a market development strategy.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that market development would let SB use capacity it is already paying for **[K]**. SB's factory runs at only 68% of capacity, so it could make considerably more toys without buying new machinery or moving to a larger site **[Ap]**. Selling those extra units abroad would spread SB's fixed costs, such as rent and machinery, across a greater number of toys, which lowers the average cost of producing each one **[An]**. A lower average cost would either widen SB's profit margin or allow it to price more competitively against toy makers already established in those two countries **[An]** A second benefit is that SB would no longer depend on a single market **[K]**. Every sale SB makes is currently in country E, where the toy market is mature and growth has run at only 2% a year **[Ap]**. Selling into two neighbouring countries with growing numbers of young children gives SB access to demand that is rising rather than flat, so it can grow without having to take customers away from established rivals at home **[An]**. Spreading sales across three countries would also mean that a fall in demand in any one of them damaged SB far less than the same fall would today, when a downturn in country E would affect all of its revenue at once **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Reed (RD)**
> 
> Reed (RD) manufactures woodwind and brass instruments in country J. Founded forty years ago, it employs 260 people and sells mainly to schools and to specialist music shops.
> 
> School music programmes in country J have been cut as education budgets have tightened, and RD's revenue has fallen steadily as a result.
> 
> **Table 1.1: RD selected data**
> 
> | Revenue in 2020 (\$m) | 38 |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue in 2025 (\$m) | 31 |
> | Employees | 260 |
> | Cost of entering the audio speaker market (\$m) | 9 |
> | Share of the speaker market held by the three largest brands (%) | 71 |
> 
> RD's board has proposed diversifying into the manufacture of high-end audio speakers, a market RD has never entered. The \$9m needed would be raised by borrowing.
> 
> RD's sales team has always sold to schools and music shops. It has no experience of selling consumer electronics.

Analyse **two** risks to RD of diversifying into the audio speaker market.
parts.solution_md:
One risk is that RD has no experience of the market it plans to enter **[K]**. RD has spent forty years making instruments for schools and music shops, and its sales team is built around those customers rather than around consumer electronics **[Ap]**. Selling speakers would mean reaching retailers and buyers RD has never dealt with, so it could easily misjudge which features customers want or how much they are willing to pay **[An]**. Mistakes of that kind are expensive here, because RD would already have spent the \$9m setting up production before discovering that the product does not sell as expected **[An]** A second risk is that RD would be entering a market already dominated by established brands **[K]**. Three companies hold 71% of the speaker market, and they have recognised names and existing shelf space that RD does not **[Ap]**. To win customers RD would probably have to price low or spend heavily on marketing, and either choice reduces the profit the new venture returns **[An]**. Because the \$9m is borrowed, RD must meet interest payments whether or not the speakers sell, so a slow start would put real pressure on a business whose revenue has already fallen from \$38m to \$31m **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Prism (PR)**
> 
> Prism (PR) is an architecture practice in country D, employing 240 people across four offices.
> 
> PR was founded by two architects who still lead it. Every design must be approved personally by one of them before it is shown to a client, and junior architects are expected to follow the practice's established style closely.
> 
> PR has won awards for the quality and consistency of its work. However, three of its largest clients have recently asked for more unusual and experimental designs, and two junior architects have left saying their ideas were never considered.
> 
> PR has never won work in the growing market for timber-framed buildings.

Explain **one** way PR's corporate culture could affect its decision-making.
parts.solution_md:
One way is that PR's culture concentrates decisions in very few hands **[1]**. Every design must be approved personally by one of the two founders before a client sees it, and junior architects are expected to follow the established style **[1]**. Ideas that do not match the founders' preferences therefore never reach a client at all, which helps explain both why two junior architects left saying their ideas were never considered and why PR has never won work in the growing timber-framed market **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Corporate culture is the set of shared values, beliefs and ways of working within a business, and it shapes which decisions are made, who makes them, and which options are considered at all
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Requiring personal approval from one of the two founders concentrates decision-making, so options not matching their preferences are filtered out before anyone else sees them
> - Expecting junior architects to follow an established style produces the consistency PR has won awards for, but narrows the range of designs the practice is willing to propose
> - Three large clients now want more experimental work, which PR's culture makes it slow to supply, so the culture that built its reputation may now be costing it business
> - Two junior architects have already left because their ideas were never considered, so the culture affects not only which decisions are taken but whether PR keeps the people who could widen its options
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Culture is invisible, so show the route by which it reaches an actual decision. Here that route runs through who is allowed to approve a design and which ideas therefore reach a client. Answers describing what a culture is like, without tracing it to a decision, rarely get past the first mark.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** feature of transformational leadership.
parts.solution_md:
One feature of transformational leadership is that the leader sets out a clear vision of what the business could become **[1]**. Rather than simply telling employees what to do, the leader explains why the change matters and how each person contributes to it **[1]**. Employees who understand and share that vision are more willing to accept difficult changes and to put in effort beyond what their job strictly requires, which is what allows a business to change direction quickly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Transformational leadership involves inspiring employees to commit to a shared vision and to perform beyond normal expectations, rather than managing them through instructions and rewards alone
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Setting out a clear vision gives employees a reason to accept change, which matters most when a business is altering direction and staff would otherwise resist
> - Leading by example builds trust, so employees are more willing to persist through difficult periods when the benefits are not yet visible
> - Paying attention to individuals and developing them raises capability as well as motivation, so the business is better able to deliver the change it wants
> - Encouraging employees to question existing methods generates ideas from the people closest to the work, which an instruction-based approach would never surface
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Leadership questions reward description of what the leader does, not what kind of person they are. Words such as inspiring or charismatic describe personality; setting a vision, explaining why change matters and developing individuals are actions. Write about behaviour and the development marks follow naturally.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Nimbus (NB)**
> 
> Nimbus (NB) installs solar panels on homes and small businesses in country A. It employs 120 people and has grown quickly.
> 
> Around 55% of NB's orders come from customers claiming a government grant that covers a quarter of the cost of installation. The government has said the grant will be reviewed next year but has not said what it will decide.
> 
> The price NB pays for solar panels has fallen by 30% in four years, but two of its three panel suppliers are based in one country, which has recently introduced new export controls.
> 
> NB's owner has begun preparing plans for several different possible futures.

Explain **one** benefit to NB of scenario planning.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that NB can prepare for outcomes it has no way of predicting **[1]**. The government has said it will review the grant that supports 55% of NB's orders, but has not said what it will decide **[1]**. By planning for both the grant continuing and the grant being withdrawn, NB can work out in advance how it would cut costs or find new customers, so it could act immediately rather than losing months of sales while it decided what to do **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Scenario planning involves preparing for several possible futures rather than forecasting a single most likely outcome, so the business is ready whichever occurs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The grant supports 55% of NB's orders and its future is genuinely unknown, so a single forecast would be a guess whereas planning for both outcomes covers either result
> - Export controls in the country where two of NB's three suppliers are based create a second uncertainty that scenario planning can address alongside the grant question
> - Agreed responses prepared in advance mean NB can act at once if the grant is withdrawn, instead of losing sales while its board works out a reply
> - Working through the scenarios may itself reveal how exposed NB is, prompting it to reduce its reliance on grant-supported orders or on suppliers in one country before anything changes
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Scenario planning does not predict the future, and answers claiming that it does tend to lose marks. Its value is preparedness: the business decides in advance what it would do under each outcome. Frame your explanation around being ready, not around knowing what will happen.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** of Porter's generic strategies.
parts.solution_md:
One of Porter's generic strategies is cost leadership **[1]**. A business following this strategy aims to produce at a lower cost than any of its competitors, usually by producing on a large scale or by using highly efficient processes **[1]**. Because its costs are lower, it can either charge the same price as rivals and earn a wider margin, or charge less and win customers while still making a profit, which higher-cost competitors cannot match for long **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Porter identified three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation and focus, applied either to a broad market or to a narrow segment
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Cost leadership means producing more cheaply than rivals, allowing either a wider margin at the same price or a lower price competitors cannot match profitably
> - Differentiation means offering something customers value that rivals do not provide, supporting a higher price and reducing the need to compete on cost
> - A focus strategy concentrates on a narrow segment and serves it better than firms treating the whole market as one, which suits smaller businesses without scale advantages
> - Porter argued that a business failing to commit to one of these becomes stuck in the middle, competing effectively on neither cost nor distinctiveness
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks about a named theory, choose one element and name it correctly. Porter's generic strategies are cost leadership, differentiation and focus. An answer gesturing at "being cheap or being different" without using the terms is unlikely to convince the examiner you know the model.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Slate (SL)**
> 
> Slate (SL) owns 26 DIY and hardware stores in country F, selling tools, paint and building materials. It employs 900 people.
> 
> SL's sales to trade customers such as builders have grown by 19% over three years, while sales to household customers have fallen by 8%. Two large online retailers now deliver tools and materials to homes across country F within a day.
> 
> SL owns all 26 of its stores rather than renting them, and has no long-term borrowing.
> 
> SL's board has never carried out a formal review of the business's position. A new managing director has asked for a SWOT analysis before deciding what SL should do next.

Explain **one** benefit to SL of conducting a SWOT analysis.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that a SWOT analysis would show SL where its real strengths lie **[1]**. SL owns all 26 of its stores outright and has no long-term borrowing, which many of its competitors could not say **[1]**. Setting that alongside the threat from next-day online delivery would help the new managing director see that SL can actually afford to invest in changing its stores, so the decision about what to do next rests on SL's real position rather than on guesswork **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
>

> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks

> 
> AO1
> 
> - A SWOT analysis sets out a business's internal strengths and weaknesses alongside the external opportunities and threats it faces, giving a structured basis for decisions
> 
> AO2
>

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'contingency planning'.
parts.solution_md:
Contingency planning is the process of preparing in advance for events that might disrupt a business **[1]**, setting out what the business would do if such an event actually happened **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Preparing plans in advance for possible emergencies or disruptions, so the business can respond quickly if they occur
> - Identifying risks that could seriously affect operations and deciding beforehand how each one would be handled
> - Planning for events that may never happen, so the business is not forced to react without preparation if they do

> **[exam-tip]**
> A contingency plan exists for something that might happen, not something that will. Your definition needs that conditional element: preparing now for an event that may occur later. A definition describing ordinary forward planning misses what makes contingency planning distinct.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'market penetration'.
parts.solution_md:
Market penetration is a growth strategy in which a business sells more of its existing products **[1]** to customers in the markets it already serves **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Selling more of a business's current products in the markets it already operates in, for example by attracting more customers or increasing purchase frequency
> - The lowest-risk strategy in the Ansoff matrix, combining existing products with existing markets
> - Growth achieved by winning a larger share of a market the business is already in, rather than by launching new products or entering new markets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Ansoff matrix sets product against market, so every strategy within it has two halves. Market penetration means existing product and existing market, and an answer naming only one of those leaves a mark behind. Whenever a term comes from a matrix, check you have covered both dimensions.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'blue ocean strategy'.
parts.solution_md:
Blue ocean strategy is an approach in which a business creates a new, uncontested market rather than competing in an existing one **[1]**, so that it faces little or no direct competition **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A strategy of creating new market space where no competitors currently operate, rather than fighting for share in a crowded market
> - An approach that makes competition largely irrelevant by offering something for which there is not yet an established market
> - Seeking growth by opening up untapped demand instead of competing directly with rivals in a saturated market

> **[exam-tip]**
> Some strategy names are metaphors, and blue ocean is one of them. The examiner is not looking for the image but for the idea behind it: creating a market with no competitors, as opposed to fighting in a crowded one. Explain the idea rather than the picture.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'PEST analysis'.
parts.solution_md:
PEST analysis is a framework used to examine the political, economic, social and technological factors outside a business **[1]**, so that it can judge how those factors may affect its plans **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A framework for examining the political, economic, social and technological influences in a business's external environment
> - A tool that identifies outside factors a business cannot control, so their likely effect on its strategy can be assessed
> - An analysis of the external conditions surrounding a business, grouped under political, economic, social and technological headings

> **[exam-tip]**
> Naming what the letters stand for shows you have learned the acronym, but a definition also needs to say what the tool is for. Add the purpose: judging how outside factors may affect the business. Frameworks produce something useful, and the second mark usually sits in what they produce.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'business strategy'.
parts.solution_md:
Business strategy is a long-term plan setting out how a business intends to achieve its objectives **[1]**, covering the whole organisation and the resources it will use to get there **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A long-term plan of action designed to achieve a business's overall objectives
> - The direction a business chooses to take, together with the way it intends to use its resources to compete successfully
> - A whole-organisation plan covering where the business wants to be in the long run and how it will get there

> **[exam-tip]**
> Strategy and tactics are easily confused. Strategy is long-term and covers the whole business; tactics are the short-term actions that carry it out. If your definition would also describe running a weekend promotion, it is describing a tactic rather than a strategy.

parts.solution_md:
Product innovation involves developing new or improved products to meet customer needs. Branding creates a distinct identity that customers associate with a business. Porter's differentiation strategy argues that businesses can compete effectively by making their products stand out in ways that justify a premium price, rather than competing purely on cost **[K]**

The Marketing Director's view has strong strategic logic. The MNCs entering KB's domestic market are likely to have significant economies of scale **[K]** and lower costs than KB, meaning that trying to match their prices would compress KB's margins without necessarily winning back customers **[An]**. KB's domestic market share has already fallen from 18% to 14% **[Ap]**, suggesting that competing on price is not a viable path. By contrast, KB has a genuine USP - its commitment to natural, sustainably sourced ingredients **[Ap]** - which larger MNCs with mass-production processes cannot easily replicate. Investing in innovation and branding that builds on this USP could attract health-conscious consumers who are willing to pay more for a product they trust, reducing the impact of price competition **[An]**

A stronger brand also increases customer loyalty **[K]**. Consumers who identify with KB's values - natural ingredients, sustainability, premium quality **[Ap]** - are less likely to switch to a cheaper MNC alternative. This makes brand investment a long-term protection against competitive pressure, not just a short-term marketing tool **[An]**

However, there are significant limitations to this approach. Brand investment and product innovation take time to influence consumer behaviour **[K]**, and KB's market share is already falling. KB's net profit declined from \$576,000 in 2022 to \$510,000 in 2023 **[Ap]** despite rising revenue, and long-term borrowings have increased significantly, suggesting limited finances for large-scale R&D or marketing spending **[An]**

KB should also consider expanding further into country Q, where export revenue has already grown by 35% **[Ap]** and the market conditions are more favourable, as an alternative route to growth that reduces reliance on the increasingly competitive domestic market

Overall, I partially agree with the statement **[E]**. Product innovation and stronger branding is the right strategic direction for KB; competing on price with MNCs is unlikely to succeed. However, it is not sufficient on its own, and the speed of KB's market share decline **[Ap]** means that faster, complementary actions,  such as a customer loyalty programme or faster investment in country Q, are also needed alongside any long-term innovation strategy  **[E]**

> - Product innovation involves developing new or significantly improved products to meet customer needs
> - Branding creates a distinct identity and set of values that customers associate with a business
> - KB's mission and commitment to natural, sustainably sourced ingredients gives it an authentic brand story that large MNCs with mass-market production processes cannot easily replicate; customers who actively choose KB because of its values are less likely to switch to a cheaper MNC alternative even when prices are lower
> - Investing in branding that communicates this authenticity more powerfully would deepen loyalty among existing customers and attract new health-conscious consumers who are willing to pay a premium for a product they trust

Using Ansoff's Matrix, Option A is a market development strategy. Option B  is related diversification, given the technological overlap between solar energy, battery storage, and EV charging** [K]**

The case for Option A is that country U's government incentives have created rapid demand for solar energy** [Ap]**, and entering early could give SES a first-mover advantage** [K]** before MNCs move in. However, SES's financial position makes this very risky. ROCE has fallen from 18% to 9% between 2018 and 2022, profit has declined every year, gearing has risen to 38%, and the acid test ratio has fallen to 0.6:1** [Ap]**,  well below the safe benchmark of 1:1. The Finance Director has already warned that any new strategy must be carefully costed. Taking on the additional capital required for international expansion - market research, regulatory compliance, building an installation team in a new country - when SES is already financially stretched would be extremely high risk** [An]**

Option B is more strategically sound. SES already has the building blocks for a strong position in EV charging: EcoGrid's energy storage expertise, the AI software platform with 12,000 paying subscribers, and an established customer base in country T** [Ap]**. Offering customers an integrated package - solar generation, energy storage, AI energy management, and EV charging - would be highly differentiated and difficult for competitors to replicate. This bundled proposition could justify premium pricing and reduce the impact of MNC price competition, rather than trying to fight MNCs on cost** [An]**

Cross-selling EV charging to existing software subscribers also reduces marketing costs, making Option B more financially efficient than winning entirely new customers** [K]**. However, the EcoGrid acquisition shows that SES can struggle when taking on new areas of expertise. Mismanaging the integration caused a loss of specialist engineers and a fall in productivity** [Ap]**. SES must ensure that EV charging investment is introduced gradually, starting with cross-selling to existing customers, rather than committing all available capital upfront **[E]**

Overall, I advise Marco to pursue Option B** [E]**. SES's financial constraints make international expansion too risky at this stage, and Option B builds on existing strengths in a way that offers genuine competitive advantage. Option A could be reconsidered once SES's finances have stabilised** [E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Using Ansoff's Matrix, Option A (existing solar product in new geographic market) is a market development strategy. Option B (EV charging in country T using SES's existing customer base and related technology) is related diversification
> - Core competencies are the unique capabilities that give a business competitive advantage
> - First-mover advantage is the competitive benefit gained by entering a market early before rivals
> - Country U's government incentives for solar energy create a genuine first-mover opportunity for SES; if SES enters country U before MNCs establish themselves there, it could build brand recognition, win key contracts, and develop local installation teams that would be difficult for later entrants to replicate quickly
> - First-mover advantage could be especially valuable given that government contracts in country T have historically delivered higher profit margins than private sector work, suggesting similar contracts in country U could help reverse SES's declining ROCE
> - However, international expansion is operationally complex for a business that relies on skilled local installation teams; unlike a product that can be manufactured and shipped, SES's core competency - designing and physically installing solar systems - is location-dependent
> - SES would need to recruit and train engineers in country U, navigate unfamiliar regulations and supply chains, and manage operations at a distance, all while its domestic financial position continues to weaken; the EcoGrid acquisition showed that SES can struggle to manage integration challenges effectively, suggesting that adding international complexity is particularly risky at this point
> - Option B offers a compelling bundled proposition that competitors would find difficult to replicate — if SES can offer customers a single integrated system covering solar generation, battery storage (via EcoGrid), AI-powered energy management software, and EV charging, it creates a highly differentiated product that pure solar companies and pure EV charging providers cannot match; this aligns with Porter's differentiation strategy and could allow SES to justify premium pricing despite increased competition from MNCs in country T

>

> 
> - SES's deteriorating financial position is the most important factor in this decision; with ROCE at 9%, profit declining for five consecutive years, gearing at 38%, and a Finance Director warning about financial weakness, taking on the capital requirements of international expansion (Option A) would carry significant risk that SES may not be able to absorb if the strategy does not deliver results quickly
> - Option B's synergies with EcoGrid's battery expertise and the existing AI software platform mean that SES is not starting from zero — it has genuine technical foundations for the EV charging market that competitors would struggle to replicate
> - However, the EcoGrid acquisition is a warning: SES took on a new area of expertise and then mismanaged the integration, losing a third of EcoGrid's specialist engineers; SES must avoid repeating this by ensuring that any EV charging investment is carefully managed, phased to match available capital, and integrated with existing operations rather than treated as a separate venture
> - Option A could remain a medium-term ambition once SES has stabilised its finances and fully integrated EcoGrid; country U's incentive-driven growth may still be accessible in two or three years
>

Use the financial data in Appendix 4 to support your argument; for example, citing the declining acid test ratio or rising gearing strengthens your analysis considerably.

>

Cash4Trash (C4T) C4T is located in the capital city of country A in Africa. This private limited company was started six years ago by Andy and Kris, who both had experience working for a large international charity. C4T is a social enterprise, initially financed by international charities and a grant from the government of country A. The government also provided land to C4T for its factory. Products are sold to local people and tourists in its shop next to the factory. C4T also sells via its website. C4T employs 90 people in its factory, who were previously unemployed. It runs training courses for 16 to 18 year olds to teach them basic skills. All profit is re-invested to expand and improve the business. C4T has won awards for being a sustainable social enterprise. Operations problems Factory employees work in teams and are rewarded with bonus payments if they exceed targets. Each team collects materials and other resources needed for production from a central store. However, sometimes this store runs out of resources, halting production. Products are checked for quality at the end of the production process and many are rejected and faults have to be corrected. Employees have been trained to specialise in one task within one team. Its products have featured in premium magazines and on websites aimed at consumers who are ‘socially responsible’. Kris works hard to keep the C4T website up-to-date and maintain its social media presence, as part of the company’s attempt to establish good customer relationships. An ambitious new idea Plastic water bottles have become a real environmental problem over recent years as more are bought and thrown away when empty. Kris is planning to introduce a new type of product. He thinks there is a market for durable, reusable plastic drinking bottles. Core competencies are the unique strengths that give a business a competitive advantage over its rivals. A true core competency must be valued by customers, give access to a range of markets, and be hard for competitors to copy **[K]**. NH has identified three core competencies: outstanding customer service, professional standards focused on efficiency, and clear leadership.

Using core competencies as a framework for strategic analysis helps NH decide which strategies are a good fit **[K]**. For example, if NH considers expanding into country Q or taking over EatBest, the core competency framework asks whether NH's strengths will transfer into these new areas. Running restaurants (EatBest) and managing hotels both require similar hospitality and operational skills, which suggests that the takeover could be a reasonable match for NH's existing capabilities **[Ap]** **[An]**

However, there is a serious problem with using NH's stated core competencies as a strategic framework. The data does not support the idea that NH currently provides outstanding customer service **[K]** **[Ap]**. Customer complaints went up by 7–9% across all hotel types in 2019, and customers often say staff are too busy to help them. Labour turnover for non-management employees doubled from 14% to 26% in one year, and job satisfaction scores are falling. This evidence suggests that NH's stated core competencies may be what Jolin hopes the business will be, rather than what it actually does well right now **[An]**

Core competency analysis is also subjective and cannot stand alone **[K]**. NH should use it alongside SWOT analysis, PEST analysis, and Porter's Five Forces to build a complete picture **[E]**

Overall, core competencies are a useful framework in principle, but for NH they are currently unreliable as a basis for major strategic decisions **[E]**. The fact that customer complaints are rising and labour turnover has nearly doubled makes it very hard to argue that "outstanding customer service" is a genuine strength that can support new strategies. If Jolin bases the decision to take over EatBest - a \$70m commitment **[Ap]** - on these flawed competencies, he risks choosing a strategy that NH does not actually have the capability to deliver. Before pursuing either the EatBest takeover or the country Q expansion, NH must first use tools like SWOT analysis **[K]** to be honest about its real weaknesses and address the HR and customer service problems that the data clearly shows. The timescale data adds to this: Option 1 can be implemented in three months, while Option 2 takes one to two years **[Ap]**. It does not mention PAC's existing quality problems, including the food poisoning incident that was not reported to directors **[Ap]**, as a restraining force for either option.
